strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine data scarcity bottleneck for RDB foundation models
Principled relational prior design with formal universality theorem (D.23) and grounded assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 19 diverse tasks with 10 random seeds and multiple evaluation protocols
Substantial efficiency gains: 3-8× faster inference, 2.6M parameters vs. 100M+ for competitors, only 2M synthetic datasets for pre-training
Fair comparison setup: providing identical DFS-linearized features to all baselines for architectural comparison
Solid theoretical treatment with rigorous proofs mapping high-level principles to constructive instantiations
Thoughtful data generation pipeline with hybrid sampling, temporal vocabulary, and practical implementation details
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: binary classification only, with multi-class and regression deferred to future work, constraining practical applicability

Contradiction between 'relational' framing and heavy reliance on DFS linearization—method converts RDB reasoning to tabular reasoning via deterministic feature engineering, undermining claims of native relational reasoning
Modest empirical improvements: averaging ~65% for RDB-PFN vs. ~64% for TabPFNv2.5 across tasks; individual task gains typically 1-3%

Synthetic data validity not established: no systematic evaluation of distribution match with real RDBs beyond visual correlation matrices; temporal vocabulary primitives (3 types) are coarse abstractions
Unfair baseline comparisons: Griffin evaluated with idealized oracle ensemble; RT's different methodology not empirically compared; graph-based RDB models relegated to appendix

Critical ablations missing: curriculum learning contribution, relational prior components (temporal vocabulary, preferential attachment, latent states), training dataset size sensitivity, and candidate set size robustness
No distribution shift analysis: how does performance degrade when real databases significantly deviate from synthetic prior distribution?
Insufficient analysis of learned patterns: no attention visualization, failure-mode characterization, or interpretation of which relational patterns the model exploits
Experimental setup biases: inconsistent baseline hyperparameter tuning, post-hoc adaptation of LimiX preprocessing, DFS engineering advantage for proposed method
Acyclic schema assumption excludes cyclic relationships present in production databases despite claim of 95% acyclicity coverage

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine scarcity of high-quality relational databases with principled PFN-based approach
Solid theoretical contribution: Comprehensive universality results extending single-table SCM completeness to multi-table case with formal proofs
Substantial efficiency gains: 3-8x faster inference, 2.6M vs 16-103M parameters, requiring only 2M vs 45-130M pre-training tasks
Comprehensive experimental setup: 19 diverse real-world RDB tasks with proper evaluation protocol (10 seeds, fair DFS-linearized comparisons)
Well-structured framework: Three-stage decomposition (Schema → Structure → Content) is principled and clearly motivated
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Paper claims to learn relational structure via relational prior, but DFS linearization completely flattens this structure into a single feature vector. Unclear why the relational prior is necessary if its benefits are discarded during linearization. Missing evidence that synthetic RDB features differ meaningfully from single-table PFN + manual RDB-aware feature engineering

Modest empirical improvements: Normalized performance ~0.89 (RDB-PFN) vs ~0.88 (TabPFN) at 1024 samples; typically <1% advantage. On many individual tasks, differences are within noise margins. 'SOTA' claim is overstated

No ablation studies: Critical design choices (temporal vocabulary injection, hybrid sampling strategy, attention-based connection sampling, two-stage curriculum) are never validated. Impossible to determine which components drive performance

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Most relevant recent work (Griffin, RT) acknowledged as incomparable; graph-based RDB methods (ContextGNN, RelGNN, RelGT) mentioned but not compared. Graph-based comparison in Appendix B.3 uses unfair 'ensemble' strategy selecting best checkpoint per task

Oversold 'Prior > Scale' narrative: 2M synthetic tasks vs 45-130M real tasks cannot support this claim due to confounding factors: synthetic vs real data fundamentally different, different pre-training methodology/architecture/ensembling, and actual performance gain is <1%

Narrow experimental scope: Only binary classification ('future work' disclaimer for multi-class/regression); 19 tasks mostly from e-commerce/web domains; applicability to finance, healthcare, scientific data unknown. Practical relevance of 64-1024 labeled examples unclear for typical RDB use cases

Synthetic data quality not validated: Figure 5 shows only visual correlation pattern similarity. No quantitative metrics comparing synthetic vs real RDBs (degree distributions, path lengths, cardinality patterns). Missing validation that schema acyclicity + locality assumptions hold across benchmarks

Negative single-table transfer unexplained: RDB-PFN underperforms specialized single-table models by 3-4% (0.617 vs 0.654), contradicting 'positive transfer' claim. No analysis of which tasks benefit vs suffer from relational pretraining

Reproducibility concerns: Code unavailable despite complexity of data generation pipeline. Many hyperparameter choices not justified. Sensitivity to design decisions (context size, curriculum balance, temporal injection ratio) unexplored

Temporal injection is ad-hoc: Specific primitives (trend, seasonality, spike) introduced without justification or ablation. No discussion of how representative these are of real temporal patterns in RDBs

strengths: Well-motivated novel problem: first foundation model for RDBs trained purely on synthetic data, addressing real scarcity of private database data
Theoretically grounded with completeness theorem (Theorem D.23) and three principled structural assumptions (acyclicity, Markovian locality, exchangeability)
Comprehensive rigorous experiments: 19 relational tasks with proper statistical evaluation (10 seeds), multiple strong baselines, efficiency comparisons
Consistent strong empirical results: outperforms single-table foundation models on relational tasks with 3-8× faster inference and 2-5% of pre-training data
Elegant three-stage decomposition (Schema→Structure→Content) with well-designed Selective SCM and curriculum learning strategy
Architectural minimalism strengthens claims: sophisticated data generation paired with simple Transformer isolates importance of relational prior
Clear block-diagonal correlation structure analysis demonstrating synthetic prior captures real RDB topology
Achieves reasonable single-table performance despite specialization, showing positive transfer from relational pre-training
weaknesses: Significant scope limitation: restricted to binary classification only, limiting real-world applicability despite being common in practice
Incomplete comparisons with relational methods: Griffin and RT comparisons use non-ideal protocols (ensemble strategy for Griffin, methodological divergence for RT) and relegated to appendix
Limited ablation studies: no systematic analysis of three-stage decomposition, curriculum learning strategy, or individual Relational Prior components
Domain gap underexplored: improvements over single-table baselines are modest on some tasks, block-diagonal structure evidence is anecdotal, no quantitative domain alignment analysis
Theoretical contributions somewhat expected: universality theorem follows standard argument from three-stage factorization; assumptions are well-known principles
Specialized single-table performance trade-off: trails specialized tabular models (Figure 4), unclear if practitioners would adopt for mixed use cases
Generalization claims need strengthening: evaluation limited to 19 tasks from two primary benchmarks, no evaluation on completely unseen database schemas
Missing error analysis: no investigation of failure modes, task characteristics predicting performance, or variance patterns across datasets
Reproducibility concerns: many implementation details scattered in appendix, LayerDAG is external component, synthetic generation involves many under-specified hyperparameters
Limited practical insights: no analysis of scaling with schema complexity, handling of schema shift, or why certain design choices (e.g., 60/90 column over-generation) matter

strengths: Novel approach to relational database pre-training using Structural Causal Models to generate synthetic data, addressing a genuine gap in foundation model research
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 19 diverse tasks with proper ablation studies, multiple evaluation protocols, and rigorous statistical analysis (10 random seeds)
Sound theoretical framework with formal mathematical definitions and completeness proofs (Theorem E.23) showing the three-stage construction can approximate any RDB distribution
Significant computational efficiency gains (2.8-4.6× faster inference) compared to single-table baseline models
Well-structured presentation of the framework with clear three-stage decomposition (Schema→Structure→Content) and detailed implementation descriptions in appendices
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Evaluation restricted to binary classification only, severely limiting real-world applicability since most RDB applications involve multi-class prediction, regression, or entity linking tasks

CRITICAL: Specialization gap unresolved—RDB-PFN consistently underperforms simpler specialized single-table models (TabPFN v2.5, TabCL) on individual tasks (Figure 4), undermining the core value proposition

Domain transfer assumption inadequately validated: while the paper claims synthetic data preserves RDB structure, there is no empirical evidence that models trained on synthetic databases learn representations that transfer to understanding real RDB structural patterns

DFS linearization of relational structures is a significant lossy simplification, but no ablation study or analysis quantifies the information loss or validates that this linearization preserves claimed relational properties

Unfair baseline comparisons: graph-based RDB methods (Griffin, RT) are not evaluated under identical protocols due to different training paradigms, making direct comparison invalid despite being claimed as alternatives
Empirical improvements are modest and inconsistent: few-shot gains (Figure 3) are often marginal and overlap with baseline confidence intervals; baselines catch up with increased context size
Key limitation (binary classification) is inadequately highlighted—discovered only in Section 7 despite being fundamental to applicability, suggesting inadequate problem scoping
Assumptions underlying theoretical completeness (Assumptions 4.1-4.3 regarding acyclicity, locality, exchangeability) are not empirically validated to hold in the actual synthetic or real datasets
Critical technical details relegated to appendices: the theoretical completeness proofs and actual architectural choices are not in the main narrative, making it difficult to assess core claims

Missing ablation on synthetic data quality: no systematic study of how synthetic data diversity, schema complexity, or distribution characteristics affect downstream performance, limiting reproducibility

strengths: Novel and important contribution: First foundation model specifically designed for relational databases, addressing a significant gap in the ML landscape where RDBs are ubiquitous but largely untouched by modern foundation model approaches

Rigorous theoretical framework with well-motivated structural assumptions (Acyclicity, Relational Markovian Locality, Conditional Exchangeability) and formal proofs of universality (Theorem E.23), providing principled design principles rather than ad-hoc engineering

Sophisticated three-stage synthetic data generation from Structural Causal Models (Schema→Structure→Content) that elegantly decomposes the RDB generation problem using LayerDAG, Selective SCMs, and Bi-Attention reasoning

Comprehensive experimental validation on 19 real-world relational tasks spanning diverse domains with rigorous evaluation protocol (10 random seeds, multiple context sizes, strict in-context learning), plus backward compatibility on 23 single-table benchmarks

Strong empirical results demonstrating single-model dominance on multi-relational tasks while maintaining competitive single-table performance, with 2.6-4.8× faster inference and only 0.7M parameters trained on ~2M synthetic tasks
Extensive ablation studies systematically testing individual components (schema generation, link generation, temporal patterns, locality assumptions) showing which design choices matter for real data
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, intuitive figures (Figure 1 overview particularly effective), rigorous but accessible technical exposition, and honest discussion of limitations
Strong reproducibility: code made available, detailed experimental setup in appendices, complete dataset statistics, all hyperparameters disclosed, demonstrating commitment to scientific transparency
Thoughtful methodological choices including two-stage curriculum learning, careful DFS linearization handling, and bi-attention design balancing schema and instance-level information
weaknesses: Evaluation restricted to binary classification only, significantly narrowing the demonstrated scope despite broader motivation; regression, multi-class, and structured prediction on RDBs remain untested, limiting practical applicability claims

Restrictive structural assumptions not empirically validated on real data: Acyclicity excludes cyclic FK relationships, Relational Markovian Locality assumes bounded-hop dependencies, and Conditional Exchangeability assumes row sharing mechanisms—no analysis of failure modes when real data violates these assumptions

Synthetic-to-real distribution gap underexplored: no explicit mismatch analysis between synthetic and real data distributions, no systematic study of which synthetic priors transfer to real data, limited isolation of what structural patterns from pretraining matter for real performance

Limited baseline comparisons: Graph-based RDB methods mentioned but not experimentally compared; comparisons mainly against classical ML and single-table TFMs; recent GNN approaches for RDBs not evaluated despite methodological relevance

Narrow evaluation breadth: 19 tasks from only 2 benchmark families (4DBInfer, RelBench) without independent RDB sources; no zero-shot evaluation on out-of-distribution schemas; generalization to different industries/domains not demonstrated

Incomplete capability assessment: only few-shot in-context learning tested without fine-tuning experiments; no evaluation on multi-hop reasoning, complex queries, aggregation accuracy, or downstream RDB tasks like anomaly detection

Shallow analysis of learned representations: limited visualization (Figure 5), no attention head analysis showing what patterns model learns, no probing studies to understand captured relational knowledge, missing feature importance analysis

Scalability and efficiency questions: memory usage not thoroughly reported, limited analysis of scaling with schema complexity, unclear behavior with 100+ tables or 1000+ columns, GPU memory requirements for different model sizes not detailed

Design choice justification: model architecture (6 layers, 128 embedding dim, 4 attention heads, feature standardization strategy) not well-motivated; task augmentation strategy (sampling 6 of 30 columns) appears arbitrary without ablation testing

Missing failure case analysis: paper doesn't deeply analyze when RDB-PFN underperforms, what happens when assumptions are violated, sensitivity to assumption violations, or minimum effective pretraining data
